_comment: RE-1 (docs/RECURRING_EVENTS_SPEC.md §5, §6.1, §16): the S14c moments block (tests/fixtures/moments_block.json, the deck as ruled) with the recurring deck under `affairs` — T1 the Arch-Chancellor's Letters, T2 the Host's Claims at two corps (P6), T3 Berthier's Memorial — exactly as §6.1 authors them, the counsel and echo lines from §12c; RE-H adds H1 the Haiti letter (§6.5) — H0 the bill alone first, `bites` on the floor half by the user's word of November 1, 2026. The shipped scenario carries this `affairs` block verbatim from RE-3 (the lockstep is pinned); the engine pins arm the real booted world with this file.

deck.title: The Bavarian Match
deck.record: Eugène, adopted by Napoleon, wed Augusta of Bavaria at Munich (historically 14 January 1806); she had been promised to Baden's heir, and Munich yielded to the Emperor's pressing.
deck.counsel: Talleyrand — A match binds Munich to the family, Sire; Baden will remember who was passed over.

deck.title: The Throne of Holland

voice.speaker: named
voice.name: Admiral Ver Huell, for the deputation of the States General

deck.record: Historically the Dutch deputation under Admiral Ver Huell asked Napoleon for a king and was given his brother Louis (5 June 1806); Grand Pensionary Schimmelpenninck resigned rather than sign. The alternative was annexation, 1810.
deck.counsel: Talleyrand — A king of your blood in Amsterdam is a king with his own treasury, Sire.

deck.title: The Crown of the Reich
deck.record: With the Confederation signed, Napoleon told Francis II to lay down the crown of the Holy Roman Empire (historically 22 July 1806); Francis did so on 6 August, and the Reich of a thousand years ended.
deck.counsel: Talleyrand — The crown is a word, Sire; but the princes read words.

deck.title: The Decree of Berlin
deck.record: Historically, from Berlin after Jena (21 November 1806), Napoleon declared the British Isles in a state of blockade and shut every port of his allies to British goods.
deck.counsel: Decrès — The Decree shuts their ports, Sire. It does not open ours.

deck.title: The Arch-Chancellor's Letters
deck.source: research #15 — Fondation Napoléon, "Walcheren et l'affaire Fouché": the Emperor's rebuke to Cambacérès for making so little use of his powers, August 1809; Malet's forged dispatch took Paris for a morning, 23 October 1812
deck.record: Historically the Emperor governed from his camp, and in August 1809 he rebuked Cambacérès for making so little use of the powers he had left him.
deck.line: Sire, the Council sits with your orders a week on the road; the clerks ask whose hand may sign what cannot wait.
deck.watch: The Emperor afield: {n} of 6 mornings — Cambacérès may write.
deck.counsel: Berthier — Every hour you give the Council, Sire, is an hour the army waits for its orders.

accept.caption: Dictate from the field
accept.echo: Cambacérès: the Council has registered the decrees Your Majesty dictated from the field.
accept.situation: The estafette carried the Emperor's dictation to Paris; the Council sits on his orders.
accept.press: PARIS — The Council of State registers the decrees His Majesty sends from headquarters.
accept.remember: In {month} you dictated from the field; Cambacérès writes again.

decline.caption: Let the Council act
decline.echo: Cambacérès: the Council has acted in Your Majesty's name; Paris will mark whose hand signed.
decline.situation: The Council of State sat under the Arch-Chancellor; Paris remarked the Emperor's absence.
decline.press: PARIS — The Arch-Chancellor presides at the Council in His Majesty's absence.
decline.remember: In {month} you let the Council act; Cambacérès writes again.

deck.title: The Host's Claims
deck.source: research #6 — Napoleon to Berthier, 14 July 1810 (Fondation Napoléon; Branda, Le prix de la gloire): war must feed war; a corps lived on the country it stood in

voice.speaker: host
voice._tenure_comment: RE-3 (RECURRING_EVENTS_SPEC.md §12c, P6): the host's minister from the cast, unless the cast's name is out of office on the issued turn — then the chancery writes. Each gap's dates are checked against its turns by the validator alone (HC-0); the engine reads turns. Hardenberg dismissed after Schönbrunn (January 1806) and recalled April 1807; Schimmelpenninck resigned when Louis was crowned (June 1806); Cevallos lost at Bayonne (May 1808).

deck.record: Historically the Emperor's rule was that war must feed war (to Berthier, 14 July 1810): a corps lived on the country it stood in.
deck.line: Sire, {seat} has quartered and fed your corps this season; the court of {host} lays its account before you.
deck.watch: {n} corps on {host}'s soil: {m} of 3 mornings — its court may present its claims.
deck.counsel: Talleyrand — An ally presents his bill once as an account, Sire. The second time, he presents it as a grievance.

accept.caption: Pay the host's claims
accept.echo: {Minister}: the account between {host} and Paris is square for the season.
accept.situation: {seat} acknowledges the payment for the army's quarters.
accept.press: {SEAT} — The court of {host} acknowledges the scrupulous payment of the army's quarters.
accept.remember: In {month} {seat} presented its account; the court of {host} writes again.

decline.caption: Live off the land
decline.situation: The army lives on the country of {host}; {seat} keeps the account.
decline.press: {SEAT} — The Grand Army is quartered upon the country of {host}.
decline.remember: In {month} the army lived on the country of {host}; its court writes again.

deck.title: Berthier's Memorial
deck.source: REFORMS_SPEC.md §6 — the law's own record, Berthier's Imperial Headquarters, expanded 1805–07; Berthier Major-General of the Grande Armée from 1805

voice.speaker: named
voice.name: Berthier, Major-General of the Grande Armée

deck.record: Historically Berthier's Imperial Headquarters grew with every campaign from 1805 into the staff that carried the Emperor's orders.
deck.line: Sire, the orders of the day leave my tent by courier; a headquarters of the Empire would carry them under its own seal.
deck.watch: At war {n} of 4 turns, and the chest could found the headquarters — Berthier may write.
deck.counsel: Daru — The Intendance can pay for clerks, Sire. It cannot pay for an order that reaches a corps a day late.

accept.caption: Found the headquarters
accept.echo: Berthier: the Imperial Headquarters is founded; the orders of the day go out under his seal.
accept.press: HEADQUARTERS — Marshal Berthier's staff becomes the Imperial Headquarters of the Grand Army.

decline.caption: Not now
decline.remember: In {month} Berthier's memorial waited; he writes again.

deck.title: The Relief of Santo Domingo
deck.source: R1 rows 1, 2, 7 (docs/audits/AFFAIRS_DESIGN_PASS_2026_10_30.md §E.1) — S1 Reyes Sánchez 2022 (Ferrand's decree of 16 Nivôse XIII); S2 the Correspondance, 29 September 1804, 5 August 1805, 26 September 1809; S4 Leissègues at San Domingo, 6 February 1806; S15 the law of 20 May 1802 and the consular acts of 16 July and 7 December 1802

voice.speaker: named
voice.name: Decrès, Minister of Marine and the Colonies

deck.record: Historically the law of 20 May 1802 kept slavery in the colonies Amiens returned, and acts of 1802 restored it in Guadeloupe and Guiana; the expedition sent to break Toussaint Louverture's rule ended in Haiti's independence, 1 January 1804.

variants.text: Historically Missiessy's squadron reached Santo Domingo on 27 March 1805 and Dessalines raised his siege the next day; it came home whole, and the Emperor thought it home too soon.

Historically Leissègues landed a thousand men at Santo Domingo and was caught at anchor on 6 February 1806: five of the line lost, 1,510 killed or wounded, 1,156 taken. The Moniteur printed a doctored account.

Historically Haiti killed the French who stayed in 1804; Ferrand's decree of 6 January 1805 let his raiders sell the Haitians they took, and Dessalines marched on Santo Domingo, killing civilians at Moca and Santiago on his retreat.

Historically Ferrand could buy twenty days' bread in February 1805 and his credit from France had not come; the Emperor ordered flour bought in America and small expeditions of muskets and men (5 August 1805).

exhibit: ‘Slavery is forever abolished.’ — the Constitution of Haiti, 20 May 1805, Article 2: three years to the day after the law.
‘Nous avons osé être libres, osons l'être par nous-mêmes et pour nous-mêmes…’ — the Act of Independence, 1 January 1804, Boisrond-Tonnerre's draft.
deck.line: Sire, Ferrand wrote {wrote} that he had bread for twenty days and no credit from France. The sea is open; two frigates can carry flour and muskets by the spring tide.
deck.watch: Blockaded {n} of the last 12 mornings — Decrès may write of Santo Domingo.
deck.counsel: Berthier — Two frigates and flour, Sire: the garrison thanks you in the spring and writes again in the autumn.

squadron.title: The Squadron for Santo Domingo
squadron.line: Sire, Ferrand wrote {wrote} that he had bread for twenty days and no credit; Your Majesty called it shameful to abandon these brave men. Brest can put five of the line to sea in a month.
squadron.counsel: Berthier — Five sail are five sail, Sire; Boulogne counts them too.

accept.caption: Send five of the line
accept.echo: Decrès: the squadron slips out of Brest on the night tide.
accept.situation: Five of the line are at sea for Santo Domingo; Decrès expects them home by {date}.
accept.remember: In {month} you sent five of the line; Decrès writes again of Santo Domingo.

home.line: The squadron is home from Santo Domingo, all five sail; Ferrand has his men, his flour and his muskets.
home.press: SANTO DOMINGO — The Emperor's squadron is home; the garrison is relieved.

caught.line: The British found the squadron at anchor off Santo Domingo: five of the line are lost; the men and the stores were ashore. Decrès asks for an inquiry.
caught.press: SAN DOMINGO — Our squadron sustained the honour of the flag against a superior enemy.

closing: Historically the Spanish colonists rose in 1808, armed by Pétion and Christophe; Ferrand killed himself after Palo Hincado on 7 November 1808, and the garrison surrendered to the British in July 1809.
Historically France recognised Haiti only in 1825, for 150 million francs paid to the former colonists; Mackau's squadron carried the ordinance, and Boyer accepted it on 11 July 1825.

accept.caption: Send flour and muskets
accept.echo: Decrès: two frigates clear Brest with flour and muskets for Santo Domingo.
accept.situation: Two frigates are at sea for Santo Domingo with flour and muskets; the garrison is provisioned by the spring.
accept.press: SANTO DOMINGO — Two frigates have carried His Majesty's flour and muskets to General Ferrand.
accept.remember: In {month} you sent flour and muskets; Decrès writes again of Santo Domingo.

decline.caption: Ferrand must hold alone
decline.echo: Decrès files Ferrand's letter; the garrison of Santo Domingo holds alone.
decline.situation: Ferrand's letter is filed at the Marine; the garrison of Santo Domingo holds alone.
decline.press: SANTO DOMINGO — General Ferrand holds the city for His Majesty.
decline.remember: In {month} you left Ferrand to hold alone; Decrès writes again of Santo Domingo.

deck.title: The Magazines
deck.source: the frontier magazines of Strasbourg, Mainz and Ulm and the field magazines of the 1805 campaign (Bertaud, 'L'armée de terre à la veille de la campagne de 1805', napoleon.org; Bergerot, Daru, intendant général de la Grande Armée); Daru Intendant-General from 1805, of the Grande Armée from October 1806 (Britannica)
deck.record: Historically the Grande Armée marched from magazines stocked before it moved — Strasbourg, Mainz and the depots raised along the road — and lived on the country only when they ran dry.

variants.text: The magazines were stocked once before; Daru asks for the convoys again.

deck.line: Sire, the magazines of the Rhine hold bread for a fortnight. Give me the sum and the convoys, and the corps will march a week without a requisition.
deck.watch: The army in the field, or a storm gathering: {m} of 2 mornings — Daru may write of the magazines.
deck.counsel: Berthier — A full magazine is a corps that arrives, Sire; an empty one is a corps that forages.

edict.name: the Magazines
edict.court_press: {SEAT} — The court of {court} contracts for its magazines.

accept.caption: Stock the magazines
accept.echo: Daru: the contracts are signed; the convoys roll for the Rhine depots tonight.
accept.situation: The magazines are stocked; the fed provinces carry a quarter more men until {until}.
accept.press: PARIS — The Intendance contracts for the magazines of the Grande Armée.
accept.remember: In {month} you stocked the magazines; Daru writes again.

decree.caption: Decree it
decree.echo: Daru: the requisitions go out under your decree; the departments fill the depots on the Emperor's word, not the Treasury's.
decree.situation: The magazines are stocked by decree; the fed provinces carry a quarter more men until {until}.
decree.press: PARIS — By imperial decree the departments requisition grain and fodder for the magazines of the Grande Armée.
decree.remember: In {month} you stocked the magazines by decree; Daru writes again.

decline.caption: Let the army forage
decline.remember: In {month} the magazines waited; Daru writes again.

deck.title: The Remounts
deck.source: the remount service of the War Administration — the Prussian horses of 1806 entrusted to Bourcier and the remount depot at Potsdam (Petre, Napoleon's Campaign in Poland); Dejean Minister of War Administration March 1802 – January 1810, then Lacuée de Cessac (napoleon.org)

voice.speaker: named
voice.name: Lacuée de Cessac, Minister of War Administration

deck.record: Historically the cavalry was remounted between campaigns by purchase and requisition — the Prussian studs after Jena, the depots that refilled the squadrons before Friedland.

variants.text: The depots were filled once before; the War Administration asks for the fairs' credit again.

deck.line: Sire, the depots hold more saddles than horses. A credit now buys remounts in the country at the spring fairs' price, not the campaign's.
deck.watch: The horse at {n}% of its establishment, depots or squadrons — the War Administration may write of remounts.
deck.counsel: Berthier — A squadron without horses is infantry that eats oats, Sire.

edict.name: the Remounts
edict.court_press: {SEAT} — The court of {court} buys remounts for its horse.

accept.caption: Buy the remounts
accept.echo: The War Administration: the remount agents ride for the fairs; the depots fill by the month's end.
accept.situation: The remounts are bought; cavalry levies cost a fifth less until {until}.
accept.press: PARIS — The War Administration buys remounts for the cavalry of the Grand Army.
accept.remember: In {month} you bought the remounts; the War Administration writes again.

decree.caption: Decree it
decree.echo: The War Administration: the departments deliver their horses under your decree; the depots fill without a sou from the Treasury.
decree.situation: The remounts come by decree; cavalry levies cost a fifth less until {until}.
decree.press: PARIS — By imperial decree the departments deliver horses to the depots of the cavalry.
decree.remember: In {month} you filled the depots by decree; the War Administration writes again.

decline.caption: Let the depots wait
decline.remember: In {month} the depots waited; the War Administration writes again.

deck.title: The Camps of Instruction
deck.source: the camps of the Army of the Ocean Coasts, 1803–05 — Boulogne and Saint-Omer under Soult, Montreuil under Ney, Bruges under Davout — raised 17 August 1805 (Bertaud, napoleon.org; history-pas-de-calais.com); Berthier Minister of War to 9 August 1807, then Clarke
deck.record: Historically the camps of Boulogne drilled a conscript army through two years of peace into the Grande Armée that marched to Ulm; a peace with camps of instruction was the Empire's habit.

variants.text: The camps were formed once before; the Minister of War asks for the grounds again.

deck.line: Sire, the regiments idle in their garrisons. Four months of camps — the Boulogne drill, the divisions manoeuvring together — would give Your Majesty an army, not a muster.
deck.watch: At peace {m} of 6 mornings, the chest idle — the Minister of War may write of the camps.
deck.counsel: Talleyrand — A camp is a peace that looks like a war, Sire; Europe will read it so.

edict.name: the Camps of Instruction
edict.court_press: {SEAT} — The court of {court} forms camps of instruction for its army.

accept.caption: Form the camps
accept.echo: The Minister of War: the camps are ordered; the first divisions march to their grounds within the month.
accept.situation: The camps of instruction are formed; every drill yields five more morale until {until}.
accept.press: PARIS — The Minister of War forms camps of instruction for the regiments of the line.
accept.remember: In {month} you formed the camps; the Minister of War writes again.

decree.caption: Decree it
decree.echo: The Minister of War: the camps are formed by your decree; the prefects quarter the divisions at the departments' charge.
decree.situation: The camps of instruction are formed by decree; every drill yields five more morale until {until}.
decree.press: PARIS — By imperial decree camps of instruction are formed for the regiments of the line.
decree.remember: In {month} you formed the camps by decree; the Minister of War writes again.

decline.caption: Let the regiments rest
decline.remember: In {month} the camps waited; the Minister of War writes again.

deck.title: The Proclamation
deck.source: the proclamation to the Grande Armée of 1 December 1805, read to the regiments on the eve of Austerlitz; Maret Minister Secretary of State to 17 April 1811, then Daru
deck.record: Historically the Emperor spoke to his army on the eve of its battles: before Austerlitz his proclamation was read at every parade, and that night the regiments lit torches of straw along the line.

variants.text: The Secretary of State asks again for the Emperor's words to the army.

deck.line: Sire, the army is in the field and the enemy before it. Words of Your Majesty's own, read at every parade at dawn, are worth a division on the day.
deck.watch: At war and afield {m} of 2 mornings — the Secretary of State may ask for a proclamation.
deck.counsel: Berthier — Read at the parade, Sire, a proclamation marches with the men.

edict.name: the Proclamation
edict.court_press: {SEAT} — The court of {court} issues a proclamation to its army.

accept.caption: Issue the proclamation
accept.echo: The Secretary of State: the proclamation is printed tonight and read at every parade at dawn.
accept.situation: The proclamation is read to the army; every drill yields five more morale until {until}.
accept.press: PARIS — The Emperor's proclamation to the Grande Armée is printed in the Moniteur.
accept.remember: In {month} you spoke to the army; the Secretary of State asks again.

decline.caption: Let the army march in silence
decline.remember: In {month} the army marched without a proclamation; the Secretary of State asks again.

deck.title: The Bank's Panic
deck.source: research — the Banque de France in the autumn of 1805: the run on its notes in Paris and its payments in specie rationed while the Treasury's cash went to the army; the Emperor back in Paris on 26 January 1806, Barbé-Marbois dismissed the next day and Mollien named to the Treasury (Mollien, Mémoires d'un ministre du Trésor public; Fondation Napoléon)

voice.speaker: named
voice.name: Regents of the Bank of France

deck.record: Historically the Bank's notes ran in Paris through the autumn of 1805 while the Treasury's cash went to the army; back from Austerlitz on 26 January 1806, the Emperor dismissed Barbé-Marbois and gave the Treasury to Mollien.
deck.line: Sire, the Bank's notes come back faster than its cellars can pay them; the Treasury owes the Bank in paper, and the regents ask to be repaid in coin.
deck.watch: The chest ran short at war {n} of the last 12 mornings — the Bank's regents may write.
deck.counsel: Gaudin — The Bank lives on the confidence it lends, Sire; repay it in coin and its notes pass at par by the spring.

accept.caption: Pay the Bank in coin
accept.echo: The regents: the Treasury's coin is in the Bank's cellars; its notes pass at par on the exchange.
accept.situation: The Treasury has repaid the Bank in coin; its notes pass at par again.
accept.press: PARIS — The Bank of France resumes its payments in specie; its notes pass at par.
accept.remember: In {month} you repaid the Bank in coin; its regents write again.

decline.caption: Let the notes fall
decline.echo: The regents: the Bank pays a part of its notes in coin; the exchange discounts the rest.
decline.situation: The Bank's notes are discounted on the Paris exchange; Paris remarks that the Treasury could not pay.
decline.press: PARIS — The Bank of France limits its payments in specie; its notes are discounted.
decline.remember: In {month} you let the Bank's notes fall; its regents write again.

deck.title: The Pope's Refusal
deck.source: research #16 (RECURRING_EVENTS_SPEC.md §6.2) — French troops in Ancona from November 1805; Napoleon to Pius VII, 13 February 1806, "You are sovereign in Rome, but I am its Emperor" (napoleon.org's wording); the Pope's refusal of March 1806 to shut his ports to the British; the Papal States annexed by the decree of 17 May 1809
deck.record: Historically French troops held Ancona from November 1805; on 13 February 1806 the Emperor wrote to Pius VII, "You are sovereign in Rome, but I am its Emperor," and in March the Pope refused to shut his ports.
deck.line: Sire, His Holiness answers that the common father of the faithful has no enemies: the ports of the Church stay open to every flag, the English among them.
deck.watch: At war with Britain: {m} of 12 mornings — Caprara may write of the Pope's ports.
deck.counsel: Talleyrand — Ancona costs a battalion and the Pope's goodwill, Sire; a refusal left standing costs the Emperor's word in every port.

accept.caption: Occupy the ports
accept.echo: Caprara: the Holy Father protests the occupation of his ports to every court of Europe.
accept.situation: French troops hold Ancona and Civitavecchia; the Pope's ports are shut to the English.
accept.press: ROME — French troops garrison the ports of the Papal States.
accept.remember: In {month} you occupied the Pope's ports; Caprara writes again.

decline.caption: Let the Pope refuse
decline.echo: Caprara: the Holy Father thanks Your Majesty; the ports of the Church stay open to every flag.
decline.situation: English goods land at Civitavecchia; the courts remark that the Pope refused the Emperor.
decline.press: ROME — English ships are seen again at Civitavecchia.
decline.remember: In {month} you let the Pope refuse; Caprara writes again.
